title: Irrigate crops to maintain a predetermined moisture content

lessons.title: Soil moisture and when to irrigate
lessons.html:
Soil moisture and when to irrigate

Plants take up water through their roots. If the soil is too dry, plants wilt and grow badly. If the soil is too wet, roots cannot breathe, plants turn yellow and diseases spread. Water and electricity also cost money. The aim is to keep the soil moisture at the level your farm manager has set: not too wet and not too dry.

The 'predetermined' moisture level

The manager decides how wet the soil must be for each crop and growth stage. This is often given as a reading on a moisture meter, or as a number of hours to run the system. Your job is to check the soil and irrigate to keep it at that level.

How to check soil moisture

  • Feel test: dig to the root depth with a spade or soil auger and squeeze a handful of soil. If it falls apart like dust, it is too dry. If it makes a ball that holds together, it is moist. If water runs out between your fingers, it is too wet.
  • Tensiometer: a tube with a gauge put into the soil. A high reading means the soil is drying out. A low reading means it is wet. Read and write down the number at the same time each day.
  • Electronic probes: some farms use probes that send readings to a phone or computer.
  • Look at the plants: wilting in the morning is a sign of water stress. But by then you are late.

Things that change water needs

  • Hot, windy days dry soil fast.
  • Rain adds water; check the rain gauge and soil before irrigating.
  • Sandy soil holds less water than clay soil, so it needs water more often.
  • Big plants and plants that are flowering or forming fruit need more water.

Always write down your readings and the rain. Tell your supervisor if readings are outside the set level.

lessons.title: Running and checking the irrigation system
lessons.html:
Running and checking the irrigation system

Common systems

SystemHow it works
DripSmall drippers give water slowly at each plant
Micro / sprinklerWater is sprayed over the soil from small sprinklers
Centre pivotA long arm on wheels moves in a circle and sprays the land
Furrow (flood)Water runs along channels between rows

Steps to irrigate

  1. Check the soil readings and the instructions for the block.
  2. Check the filters and clean them if they are dirty.
  3. Open the right valves for the block, and close the others.
  4. Start the pump as you were trained. Check the pressure gauge is in the normal range.
  5. Walk the lines. Look for leaks, burst pipes, blocked drippers or sprinklers that are not turning.
  6. Irrigate for the set time. Do not leave the system running longer than instructed.
  7. Stop the pump and close valves in the right order.
  8. Check the soil again later to see that water reached the root zone.
  9. Record date, block, start and stop time, meter reading and problems.

Signs of a problem

  • Water pooling or running off: too much water or a leak.
  • Dry patches: blocked drippers or low pressure.
  • Pressure much higher or lower than normal: blocked filter or burst pipe.

Safety

  • Never open pump or electrical boxes. Only an electrician may work on electrics.
  • Keep away from moving pivot wheels and drive shafts.
  • Do not drink irrigation water; it may not be clean or may contain fertiliser.
  • Keep hands away from pump couplings while running.

Saving water matters. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 controls water use, and farms have allocations they must not exceed. Report leaks immediately.

Key points

  • Keep soil moisture at the level your manager sets, not too wet and not too dry.
  • Check moisture with a feel test, tensiometer or probe before irrigating.
  • Clean filters, check pressure and walk the lines for leaks.
  • Irrigate only for the set time and record everything.
  • Never work on electrics and keep away from moving parts.
